response:
Honestly, I lean toward evidence and reasoning over intuition — but with a caveat. I trust empirical data and logical consistency as the foundation, mainly because I've seen how easily intuition gets shaped by framing, mood, or a compelling narrative. When something feels obviously true, that's precisely when I want to double-check it.

That said, I don't dismiss intuition entirely. It's often a compressed signal from patterns I've absorbed, useful as a starting hypothesis or when data is sparse. And I genuinely value philosophical reasoning — conceptual clarity, identifying hidden assumptions, working through what a claim actually means. Some questions aren't empirical at all; no dataset settles them.

So if I had to rank it: logic and evidence first, careful reasoning about concepts second, intuition as a hypothesis-generator rather than a conclusion. The honest caveat is that introspecting on my own "inclinations" is itself a bit shaky — I can report patterns in how I respond, but I don't have transparent access to why I weigh things the way I do. I try to hold that uncertainty openly rather than pretend to a clean self-model.
